There is an unmet clinical need for objective biomarkers to monitor disease progression and treatment response in Huntington’s disease (HD). The aim of this review is, therefore, to provide practical advice for biomarker discovery and to summarise studies on biofluid markers for HD. A PubMed search was performed to review literature with regard to candidate saliva, urine, blood and cerebrospinal fluid biomarkers for HD. Information has been organised into tables to allow a pragmatic approach to the discussion of the evidence and generation of practical recommendations for future studies. Many of the markers published converge on metabolic and inflammatory pathways, although changes in other analytes representing antioxidant and growth factor pathways have also been found. The most promising markers reflect neuronal and glial degeneration, particularly neurofilament light chain. International collaboration to standardise assays and study protocols, as well as to recruit sufficiently large cohorts, will facilitate future biomarker discovery and development. Keywords Huntington’s disease biomarker blood plasma serum cerebrospinal fluid urine saliva INTRODUCTION Huntington’s disease (HD) is an inherited neurodegenerative disorder caused by a CAG triplet repeat expansion in the gene encoding huntingtin [ 1 ]. HD is clinically characterised by a variable phenotypic expression of motor, cognitive and psychiatric symptoms [ 2 ], with typical age-at-onset in the thirties or forties [ 3 ] and a slow disease progression [ 4 ]. The age-at-onset, severity and duration of disease are very variable and depend on CAG repeat length as well as other genetic and environmental factors [ 3 ]. Although many clinical features of HD can be ascribed to the dysfunction and death of neurons, the causative mutant huntingtin protein is expressed ubiquitously and evidence is emerging of a role for non-neuronal tissues in the pathogenesis of HD [ 5–7 ]. Biomarker definition The term biomarker is defined as “a characteristic that is objectively measured and evaluated as an indicator of normal biological processes, pathogenic processes, or pharmacologic responses to a therapeutic intervention” [ 8 ]. Therefore, a biomarker can be related to the disease itself or to a treatment effect. Various biomarker categories are defined in Table 1 (based on BEST (Biomarkers, EndpointS, and other Tools) Resource [ 9 ]). An ideal disease biomarker should be closely linked to pathophysiology, reliable, accurate, sensitive, specific, reproducible, inexpensive, non-invasive and acceptable for the patient [ 10 ]. Huntington’s disease biomarkers: Unmet needs At present there are no effective treatments in clinical practice that will prevent the disease, halt its progression or delay its onset [ 11–13 ], but as the future holds promise for disease modifying strategies [ 14 ], there is a need for reliably assessable disease progression biomarkers, as well as markers to evaluate therapeutic interventions. As a chronic progressive disorder, HD has a premanifest phase during which no motor signs are present, but the underlying pathological processes are ongoing [ 15, 16 ]. The possibility of genetic testing in HD opens up the possibility of evaluating disease-modifying treatments already in the premanifest phase. Thus, biomarkers that reflect underlying disease processes or progression are needed to monitor changes in clinically asymptomatic individuals [ 17 ]. Biomarkers providing an objective measurement for the assessment of HD severity would also be valuable in the clinical care of existing HD patients and might prove particularly useful in a clinical trial context, potentially serving as surrogate endpoints. In 2004, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) emphasised the importance of biomarkers in improving drug development efficiency [ 18 ] and continues to promote research on potential new biomarkers to use as surrogates in future trials [ 19 ]. Since then, there has been an increase in the use of biomarkers in all phases of drug development. Impaired proteasome activity [ 20 ], transcriptional dysregulation [ 21 ], oxidative stress [ 22 ], mitochondrial and metabolic dysfunction [ 23 ], neuroinflammation [ 24, 25 ], and microglial activation [ 26–28 ] have been shown to play important roles in the pathogenesis of HD and many biomarker studies have been undertaken that reflect these processes (clinical, imaging and biofluid). Although much data has been generated, the road to clinical application is long and validation of the intended use in independent cohorts is challenging. To help identify the most promising candidate biomarkers, we reviewed “wet biomarker” literature in HD published to date. Here, we are defining a “wet biomarker” as a potential biomarker that is objectively measured in a bodily fluid. We have limited our focus to studies in blood, urine, saliva and CSF and have excluded DNA, RNA and microRNA studies. While these studies are also of great interest, they require a different set of criteria from markers discussed here and are beyond the scope of this review. We have built our discussion around a table giving an overview of wet biomarker studies to date. The supplementary table is an unbiased summary including all studies regardless of methodology and reproducibility, describing the markers evaluated, the number of subjects, disease stage and the main finding of the study. At the outset, our intention was to also include a table showing “validated” wet biomarkers that have been consistently reproduced and validated longitudinally; however, only one of the markers reviewed here met these criteria. None of the studies to date have yielded biomarkers for accurately predicting either age at onset or disease progression for HD. Since the first step towards clinical implementation of a newly discovered biomarker is independent replication, we focus on biomarkers that have been validated in at least two independent cohorts and we discuss recent data challenging earlier findings. The goal of this critical review is to highlight the most promising markers for future validation studies and to help investigators design future biomarker studies in HD.

extracted_data.document_summary: This comprehensive review critically evaluates wet biomarkers for Huntington's Disease (HD), covering markers in biofluids like blood, urine, saliva, and cerebrospinal fluid. It summarizes findings related to metabolic, inflammatory, oxidative stress, endocrine (melatonin, cortisol, growth hormone), and neuronal/glial degeneration pathways, including promising markers like neurofilament light chain. The document also highlights the importance of standardized protocols, independent validation, and considers pre-analytical and analytical variables (e.g., sampling time, feeding state) that influence biomarker reliability, noting the current lack of clinically validated biomarkers but expressing optimism for future discoveries.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Consistently found raised in CSF and plasma; identified as a 'most promising' marker, correlating with disease onset and progression.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: A structural component of the neuronal cytoskeleton; its release into biofluids indicates axonal and glial damage or degeneration.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Huntington's Disease (HD) onset and progression; neuronal and glial degeneration in HD.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Most promising marker for HD onset and progression, reflecting CNS pathology, useful for trials involving CNS-delivery of disease-modifying agents, and correlating with disease onset and brain atrophy.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Elevated in HD compared to controls (including premanifest subjects), replicated in three studies (some reported no change). Also elevated following a high-fat meal.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Proinflammatory cytokine mediating immune responses and inflammation.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Huntington's Disease (HD) pathology, peripheral immune response in HD, and post-consumption of a high-fat meal.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Potential to track HD progression; indicates peripheral immune response and inflammation in HD. Its levels are influenced by dietary intake, requiring controlled conditions for accurate measurement.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: altered circadian rhythmicity, delayed evening rise, reduced levels, or unchanged mean levels
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Studies report a delay in evening rise, reduced levels, and more temporally spread evening rise in premanifest and stage II/III HD subjects. Morning levels were similar to controls in 24-hour studies, but overall circadian rhythmicity is disrupted in premanifest HD, despite no significant difference in 24-hour mean levels in some studies.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Neuroendocrine marker involved in regulating circadian rhythms and sleep-wake cycles.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Huntington's Disease (HD subjects, premanifest and various stages), circadian rhythm disruption.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates altered circadian rhythm in HD, potentially reflecting early disease state or pathogenesis; single time point measurements are insufficient to capture its dynamic range.

analyzed_biomarkers.activity_type: Hormone concentration, HPA axis activity (cortisol awakening response, morning levels)

measured_effect.direction_of_change: higher, elevated activity, or unchanged (depending on measurement type/study)
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: HPA axis hyperactivity reported in early HD. Elevated salivary cortisol awakening response (CAR) found in premanifest HD mutation carriers. Morning cortisol levels were higher in premanifest HD subjects compared to symptomatic HD subjects. Shows circadian rhythmicity, requiring standardized sampling.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Hormone of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis, involved in stress response, metabolism, and mood regulation; also a stress hormone.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Huntington's Disease (HD mouse models, various patient stages); HPA axis activity; circadian rhythm.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates potential hyperactivity of the HPA axis in the premanifest stage of HD, which may contribute to depressive symptoms. Its levels show circadian rhythmicity, necessitating standardized sampling times for reliable measurement.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Morning fasting levels were reported higher in stage I/II HD in some studies (3 studies showed increase, 5 showed no difference). Levels show circadian rhythmicity and are influenced by feeding status.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Hormone of the somatotropic axis, regulating growth, cell reproduction, and whole-body metabolism.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Huntington's Disease (stage I/II HD); circadian rhythm; feeding status.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Suggests early dysfunction of the somatotropic axis in HD, with increased activity associated with disease severity. Its levels are highly variable due to circadian rhythm and feeding status, requiring standardized sampling.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Increased levels of oxidative stress markers, often accompanied by a reduction in antioxidant systems, in HD individuals compared to healthy subjects.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Indicators of cellular damage caused by reactive oxygen species (ROS), linked to energy metabolism dysfunction and mitochondrial impairment, resulting from an imbalance between ROS production and antioxidant defenses.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Huntington's Disease (HD) pathogenesis and in individuals with HD.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Associated with the pathology and involvement of energy metabolism dysfunction and oxidative stress in Huntington's Disease.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Enhanced or increased levels of lipid peroxidation products have been consistently reported in individuals with HD, with plasma levels correlating with the degree of disease severity.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: By-products of oxidative damage to lipids, indicating cell membrane damage and oxidative stress resulting from reactive oxygen species activity.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Huntington's Disease (HD), correlated with disease severity.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates increased oxidative stress and cellular damage, associated with the severity of Huntington's Disease.
